question: A grants officer reads a Claude-written explainer of a funding scheme and notices that it gives one closing date in the opening paragraph and a different closing date three paragraphs later. What should she do first?
options: A) Ask Claude which of the two dates it meant, and use whichever one it settles on when it is asked to resolve the conflict.
B) Delete the earlier paragraph so the explainer no longer contradicts itself, and circulate the corrected version today.
C) Go back to the funder's own published scheme rules and establish which closing date, if either of them, is the real one.
D) Keep the later of the two dates on the basis that it was written after Claude had processed more of the scheme material.
correct_answers: C) Go back to the funder's own published scheme rules and establish which closing date, if either of them, is the real one.
explanations: Asking the same conversation to arbitrate treats Claude as a singular source of truth on exactly the point where it has already demonstrated it is unreliable, and it will produce a confident answer either way.

Removing one of the two dates makes the internal contradiction disappear without resolving it, which is worse than leaving it visible: the surviving date may well be the wrong one, and the warning sign has been erased.

Correct. An internal contradiction shows at least one statement is unreliable, and it cannot be settled inside the response. Checking the funder's own published rules resolves it against an authoritative source rather than relying on Claude alone.

Position in a response carries no evidential weight; a later sentence is not better sourced than an earlier one. Picking a date by where it appeared leaves the officer publishing a deadline she has never verified.
